name: Meta Beaver Dam
heading: 3. Meta Beaver Dam — 220 MW Projected Peak Demand; Under Construction
brief: Meta announced its first Wisconsin data center in Beaver Dam, Dodge County , on November 12, 2025. The planned AI-optimized campus will contain more than 700,000 square feet of facilities and represents at least $1 billion in investment . Alliant Energy’s initial project announcement anticipated roughly 1,000 construction jobs at peak and more than 100 long-term operational roles, with the data center expected to come online in 2027. The 220 MW figure comes from utility filings and Wisconsin Watch’s examination of the Public Service Commission’s May approval of Alliant’s service agreement. The regulator modified the agreement and scrutinized how costs would be allocated to other customers. That projected peak does not establish that 220 MW of servers are energized in October 2026. Some market inventories use a larger gross development envelope; without matching phase definitions, those figures should not be added to this entry’s utility-demand number. Milwaukee Journal Sentinel’s April 7, 2026 aerial video documents construction at Meta’s Beaver Dam data center.
articleTitle: Top 3 Largest Data Center Projects in Wisconsin (2026)

name: Microsoft Fairwater, Mount Pleasant
heading: 2. Microsoft Fairwater, Mount Pleasant — About 450 MW Tracked; First Facility Operating
brief: Microsoft announced on June 23 that its first Fairwater facility in Mount Pleasant was fully operational after equipment began coming online in April. The large AI computing campus occupies land once associated with Foxconn’s much smaller-than-promised Wisconsin manufacturing expansion. Microsoft said the first facility was supporting nearly 550 full-time jobs at the June milestone and that its second adjacent facility was under construction for anticipated completion in 2028. Microsoft’s public release does not provide a comparable present critical-IT megawatt measurement for its Mount Pleasant building. A separate infrastructure-tracking model associates roughly 450 MW of campus-scale power with Fairwater and around 370 MW of estimated energized power; both are independent modeled figures, not Microsoft-certified measured consumption . An older regulatory discussion also involved larger multi-building load forecasts that should not be treated as one completed facility. The operator’s more directly verifiable numbers concern the first building’s opening, site jobs and spending. Aero

name: Vantage Lighthouse, Port Washington
heading: 1. Vantage Lighthouse, Port Washington — 902 MW Critical IT Planned; Construction Underway
brief: The largest disclosed site-level critical IT plan in this selection is Vantage Data Centers’ Lighthouse campus near Lake Michigan in Port Washington. The company describes four data center buildings spanning 2.5 million square feet across 672 acres , with a planned 902 MW of critical IT load and targeted full completion in 2028. It is being developed to serve Oracle and OpenAI’s Stargate infrastructure. A different roughly 1.3 GW figure appears in electrical interconnection planning; that is not an additional operating data center or 1.3 GW of running chips. Vantage’s 2025 announcement projected more than $15 billion of investment. By 2026, construction was underway and local coverage reported progress on multiple large buildings. But project financing, construction milestones, site access and the final availability of electricity are separate matters. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources says the campus requires wetland, stormwater and air-emissions reviews, with a separate state review of the proposed transmission interconnection. name: Vantage Project Latigo, Laramie County
heading: 3. Vantage Project Latigo, Laramie County — 480 MW Proposed; Rezoning Approved
brief: Vantage Data Centers is seeking to develop Project Latigo on approximately 1,835 acres along Terry Ranch Road, about 12 miles south of Cheyenne. The project is described as a roughly 480 MW initial campus , with discussion of potential future expansion. A September 1, 2026 Laramie County commissioners meeting approved the land-use change to a Planned Unit Development on a unanimous vote. That authorizes a zoning framework; it does not mean data halls are built, a tenant has signed, or 480 MW is energized. The project’s public record describes proposed on-site natural-gas generation and a closed-loop cooling design. Vantage has discussed a requirement that the development restore more water than it uses, and county residents have asked how those promises would be monitored and enforced. Its construction timetable has been described as starting in 2027 and extending into 2030, contingent on further permits, detailed designs and power arrangements. The county planning map shows development areas and open-space buffers, but a mapped parcel is not a construction completion photograph. Van

name: Prometheus Hyperscale Evanston
heading: 2. Prometheus Hyperscale Evanston — 1.25 GW Initial Plan; County Permits Approved
brief: Prometheus Hyperscale is pursuing a 1.25 GW initial data center campus on approximately 506 acres east of Evanston in Uinta County. The developer has promoted a possible path to 5 GW through later expansion, but that larger number is not part of today’s initial ranking. On June 16 , county commissioners unanimously approved the conditional-use permit for the data center, according to the company’s June 17 announcement . The campus is designed around an islanded, or off-grid, power system using gas engines and turbines rather than relying exclusively on the existing public utility connection. In September, local reporting recorded county approval for the power-facility permit , following the planning commission’s August recommendation. These decisions support the project’s progress, but they do not demonstrate that the entire generating plant, air permits, data halls, tenant contracts or financing are completed. name: Google Project Tembo, Cheyenne
heading: 1. Google Project Tembo, Cheyenne — 2.7 GW Power-Resource Mix; Pre-Construction
brief: Google’s Project Tembo , located in the Switchgrass Industrial Park approximately eight miles south of Cheyenne, is tied to Wyoming’s largest disclosed data center power arrangement. The site was formerly Project Jade , a Crusoe-and-Tallgrass development initially described as a 1.8 GW computing project. Crusoe exited during 2026, and Google subsequently advanced a revised four-building concept. In September, the company presented the community with a planned investment of approximately $17 billion , according to Wyoming Public Media’s report on Google’s public meeting . On October 6 , utility provider Black Hills Corp. announced definitive power agreements effective September 30 and running through 2048. The arrangement covers approximately 2.7 GW of total resources, including reserve margins : up to 590 MW from grid-connected service and 2.1 GW of third-party contracted resources managed through a private microgrid. Black Hills proposes to invest about $1.8 billion in new gas generation. The 2.7 GW headline is the total electricity-resource mix, not Google’s stated critical IT load

name: Tract Caldwell Valley, Texas
heading: 10. Tract Caldwell Valley, Texas — 4 GW Site Capacity
brief: Tract’s Caldwell Valley Technology Park comprises nearly 3,000 acres in Caldwell County with roughly 4 GW of marketed development capacity . The campus combines planned data-center plots with prospective transmission and natural-gas infrastructure, but the master-plan number does not represent a signed four-gigawatt supply contract. Tract’s own development materials identify an initial smaller substation program and future energization rather than completed full-build service. Early phases are far easier to validate than the ultimate 4 GW figure. The Texas Top 7 explains the distinction and how Caldwell compares with Fermi, Galaxy and IREN. Caldwell Valley ties Joule at approximately 4 GW in the chart. A later commissioned-capacity ranking could produce a dramatically different order.

name: Joule High-Performance Compute Campus, Utah
heading: 9. Joule High-Performance Compute Campus, Utah — 4 GW Energy Plan
brief: Joule Capital Partners and Caterpillar have publicized a four-gigawatt total-energy design for a high-performance compute campus in Utah. Their approach centers on gas-powered distributed generation, integrated cooling and recovery of waste heat from equipment, rather than depending solely on distant grid deliveries. The arrangement is a significant equipment and development proposal, but that does not establish that 4 GW of generators are installed, financed and operating today. Important unknowns include phasing, fuel arrangements, emissions conditions and data-center tenancy. Joule is examined in the Utah state rankings . Its engineering merits should ultimately be judged by delivered power, usable waste heat, water consumption, air permits and operational efficiency.
articleTitle: Top 10 Largest Data Center Energy Projects in America (2026)

name: Homer City Energy Campus, Pennsylvania
heading: 8. Homer City Energy Campus, Pennsylvania — Up to 4.4 GW Planned Power
brief: The redevelopment of Pennsylvania’s retired Homer City coal station is designed around up to 4.4 GW of natural-gas electricity generation for AI data centers and possible grid service. Some permitting and coverage use approximately 4.5 GW or a different equipment nameplate figure, illustrating how turbine ratings and project design assumptions can vary. Site redevelopment and generating-plant work have advanced, but a prospective power plant is not the same as commissioned megawatts or leased data halls. Regulatory decisions, fuel contracts and connection arrangements will decide how much electricity can actually be delivered. More context appears in the Pennsylvania Top 3 . The project would be an important example of industrial-site reuse if its generating and computing plans reach commercial operation.
articleTitle: Top 10 Largest Data Center Energy Projects in America (2026)

name: Meta Hyperion, Louisiana
heading: 7. Meta Hyperion, Louisiana — 5 GW Planned Compute Capacity
brief: Meta announced that its Richland Parish investment is being expanded toward 5 GW of compute capacity . Hyperion is already a major construction effort with associated transmission and electricity-supply work. The company’s target measures an eventual compute development scale, not proof of five gigawatts of operating servers in 2026. Unlike an independent power producer, Meta is chiefly developing computing infrastructure and arranging the electrical service necessary to run it. The ultimate grid and generation mix should therefore be accounted for separately from the compute figure. The Louisiana state ranking describes how the project compares with other regional proposals. A useful next milestone would be a verified public accounting of installed IT megawatts alongside dedicated supply and transmission upgrades.
articleTitle: Top 10 Largest Data Center Energy Projects in America (2026)

name: E2B4 Roswell Information Park, New Mexico
heading: 6. E2B4 Roswell Information Park, New Mexico — 6.5 GW Proposed Generation
brief: E2B4’s proposed Roswell Information Park separates its engineering targets more clearly than many developers: its investor materials call for 6.5 GW of net islanded generation supporting 4,960 MW of critical IT capacity across 20 halls. That difference is important because the generators must also cover equipment losses, cooling requirements and reliability reserves. The developer describes gas-supply access and a phased initial compute program, but the full buildout still depends on engineering, contracts, environmental permits and financing. The scale is a proposal, not installed generating capacity. The New Mexico state ranking compares Roswell with Project Jupiter and Meta Los Lunas. Its 6.5 GW generation figure is the value plotted in the national chart, rather than its lower 4.96 GW planned IT load.
articleTitle: Top 10 Largest Data Center Energy Projects in America (2026)

name: Nscale Monarch Compute Campus, West Virginia
heading: 5. Nscale Monarch Compute Campus, West Virginia — Over 8 GW Power Runway
brief: Nscale’s proposed Monarch campus in Mason County has a long-term microgrid expansion runway exceeding 8 GW , according to its March announcement. The site has a state-certified development framework, but the large figure represents possible phased expansion rather than currently available electricity. Early project reporting described a much smaller roughly 2 GW first-phase ambition. Gas generation, power delivery, data halls and customers would need to be built and contracted in stages. This creates a meaningful difference between a large permitted development zone and a reliable energy supply. The earlier West Virginia ranking also compares Monarch with the separate Tamarack and Ridgeline projects. The headline 8 GW-plus figure is best read as a development ceiling whose eventual delivery depends on permitting, capital and secured equipment.
articleTitle: Top 10 Largest Data Center Energy Projects in America (2026)

name: PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, Ohio
heading: 4. PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, Ohio — 8 GW Planned IT Load
brief: OpenAI says its partnership with SB Energy, NVIDIA and the U.S. Department of Energy targets approximately 8 GW of critical IT capacity near Piketon, at and around the former Portsmouth uranium-enrichment site. That figure measures electricity intended for computing equipment; the corresponding facility-level power requirement would be greater after cooling, power distribution and other overhead. NVIDIA initially backed 4.25 GW-IT of land, power and shell capacity, with an option tied to the remaining 3.75 GW-IT. Pike County describes phased future delivery and ongoing community agreements. The scale is extraordinary, but it is not eight gigawatts of power plants already available. The Ohio ranking distinguishes these commitments from 2026 energized load. The most revealing future numbers will be completed substations, service contracts, installed cooling systems, and audited IT power in each commissioned phase.
articleTitle: Top 10 Largest Data Center Energy Projects in America (2026)

name: Stratos / Wonder Valley, Utah
heading: 3. Stratos / Wonder Valley, Utah — About 9 GW Long-Term Concept
brief: The Stratos Project Area in Box Elder County has been described by Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority at approximately 9 GW of long-run project scale. The developer’s more detailed Wonder Valley Utah disclosure discusses approximately 7.5 GW over later stages, while an October water application outlines fifteen 500 MW natural-gas blocks. The 7.5 GW detailed generation proposal should not be confused with the higher 9 GW development ambition . Local land-use actions have advanced, but air and water approvals, financing and actual plant construction remain central uncertainties. Those questions, including water sourcing and power-plant emissions, matter as much as the announced scale. The full Utah report documents the competing figures. Video thumbnail from the April 27, 2026 Box Elder County commission meeting recording , which discusses the Stratos proposal and local oversight.

name: Creekstone Delta Gigasite, Utah
heading: 2. Creekstone Delta Gigasite, Utah — More Than 10 GW Power Stack
brief: Creekstone Energy says its proposed Delta Gigasite combines natural gas, solar and storage resources into a power stack exceeding 10 GW . The company’s breakdown includes 2.1 GW natural gas and 6 GW solar, along with storage and other resources. Storage capacity and intermittent solar nameplate output are not the same as continuous round-the-clock generation. The site has industrial zoning, an executed gas interconnect agreement and initial work in progress. Creekstone’s own compute specifications separately cite approximately 4.61 GW of HPC load. These distinctions are why a 10 GW power stack must not be presented as ten gigawatts of functioning computers. See the Utah ranking . Future reporting should isolate dispatchable gas generation, solar nameplate capacity, energy-storage power and duration, and the megawatts actually delivered to tenants.
articleTitle: Top 10 Largest Data Center Energy Projects in America (2026)

name: Fermi Project Matador, Texas
heading: 1. Fermi Project Matador, Texas — 11 GW Power Campus
brief: Fermi’s Project Matador near Amarillo is pursuing a vast, phased mix of natural gas, potential nuclear generation and grid-connected resources. The 11 GW headline describes an ultimate energy-campus design rather than installed power plants or operating data halls. Fermi’s latest annual report retains an 11 GW goal for the principal campus while describing possible expansion on additional acreage. A 222 MW proposed TensorWave tenant arrangement is much smaller than the full master plan, and its closing had been extended to October 31. Fermi has disclosed delays to its earlier power-ramp schedule. That means the most significant near-term measures are a closed tenant agreement, financed construction, equipment commissioning and real megawatts available for use. The Texas Top 7 examines these stages in detail. The full chart design and methodology notes are also available in the Chart Atlas . The chart measures the magnitude of disclosed ambitions, not the probability that each buildout will finish.
